sections.h2: What does homestead exemption mean in Connecticut?
sections.html:
In Connecticut law, a homestead exemption is a shield against creditors. It is not a discount on the property tax bill. The rule sits in the postjudgment chapter of the General Statutes, section 52-352b, and it limits what a judgment creditor can reach in a home.

People often search for the phrase hoping to lower a tax bill, so the two ideas are worth separating. Tax relief for older, disabled, blind or veteran owners comes from other statutes with other names, covered further down.

sections.h2: How much of a home is protected from creditors?
sections.html:
The current statute protects the homestead of the exemptioner up to a value of $250,000. Value is the fair market value of the real property less any statutory or consensual lien on it. A smaller limit of $75,000 applies to money judgments that arise from a claim of sexual abuse or exploitation of a minor, sexual assault or other wilful, wanton or reckless misconduct by a natural person.

The amount used to be much lower. The history note under the statute shows that Public Act 93-301 first set the figure at $75,000 in 1993, that a 2003 act added $125,000 for judgments tied to hospital services, and that Public Act 21-161 replaced both with the $250,000 figure. An appellate annotation in the same chapter says the larger exemption applies in bankruptcy and postjudgment proceedings begun on or after October 1, 2021, whenever the underlying debt arose.

The statutes page notes that a 2026 supplement carries amendments passed in the 2025 sessions. Check the current text or ask a Connecticut attorney before you rely on a dollar figure.

sections.h2: What counts as a homestead under the statute?
sections.html:
A homestead is owner-occupied real property, a co-op, or a mobile manufactured home used as a primary residence. That definition is in section 52-352a(5). Co-ops were added by Public Act 10-181 and mobile manufactured homes by Public Act 94-55, according to the history note.

  • Owner-occupied: a house you rent to someone else is not a homestead for this purpose.
  • Primary residence: a second home or a vacation property does not qualify.
  • Exemptioner: the person claiming the exemption must be a natural person, so a house held in an LLC is outside the definition.

An inherited house you do not live in is not your primary residence, so the shield may not apply to it. An attorney can sort out facts like that.

sections.h2: Does the exemption protect a home from a mortgage or a foreclosure?
sections.html:
No. A mortgage is a consensual lien, and the statute measures the exemption after subtracting liens. Court annotations under section 52-352b say a mortgage is not subject to the homestead exemption, and one decision held that a waiver given voluntarily and with a lawyer's help was not against public policy.

The same annotations touch on sale proceeds. After a foreclosure sale is confirmed and reduced to proceeds, homestead exemption rights attach to those proceeds, according to one appellate ruling. Another ruling found that a trial court lacked subject matter jurisdiction to act on a homestead claim meant to protect proceeds of a voluntary sale from a judgment lien creditor.

For a homeowner who is behind on payments, that means the exemption is not a way to stop a lender. It speaks to what an unsecured creditor can take. If the problem is a mortgage in default, the options are a loan modification, a sale, or a deal with the lender, and a cash sale can close faster than a listing. Talk with an attorney or a HUD-approved housing counselor about where you stand before you sign anything.

sections.h2: Which Connecticut property tax breaks look like a homestead exemption?
sections.html:
Connecticut's exemptions for owners are listed in section 12-81 of the General Statutes, and several are fixed-dollar reductions in assessed value. The ones that most resemble a homestead exemption are tied to who the owner is.

  • Blind residents: property to the amount of $3,000 under subdivision (17).
  • Veterans who served in wartime: property to the amount of $1,000 under subdivision (19).
  • Service members and veterans with disability ratings: property up to $3,500 under subdivision (20).

The statute makes these subject to filing rules in other sections, and the exemptions also have limits when a person qualifies under more than one category. Your town assessor takes the application, so call that office for forms and deadlines. The circuit breaker credit already described on this page also runs through the assessor.

sections.h2: Does a tax relief program change the conveyance tax when I sell?
sections.html:
It can. The Department of Revenue Services lists an exemption from the state conveyance tax for the principal residence of a seller who is approved for property tax assistance under section 12-129b or 12-170aa for the current assessment year, or who was approved within the prior 15 months or less. The DRS page adds that such a deed is not exempt from the municipal portion.

The same list covers other cases that come up in distressed sales.

  • A deed in lieu of foreclosure on the seller's principal residence.
  • A principal residence sold for a price too low to pay the mortgages and the tax liens that rank ahead of them.
  • A principal residence with a crumbling foundation caused by pyrrhotite, if a professional engineer has evaluated it in writing and the owner is not getting help from the Crumbling Foundations Assistance Fund. That exemption applies to the first transfer after the written evaluation.

An estate of a person who was approved for tax assistance cannot claim the first exemption.

sections.h2: What does the conveyance tax cost when a Connecticut house is sold?
sections.html:
The base state rate is three-quarters of one percent of the price, and the municipal rate is one-quarter of one percent. Both come from section 12-494. The tax applies when the consideration equals or exceeds $2,000, and the statute sets a higher state rate of one and one-quarter percent for property that is not residential, except unimproved land. Other rates apply to certain residential estates, so read the statute or ask the town clerk about a high-value sale.

The grantor, the grantor's attorney or an authorized agent files Form OP-236, and the tax is paid when the deed is recorded. Many towns take the return and payment online through myCTREC. In towns that do not, the grantor submits the paper form to the town clerk with a check made out to the Commissioner of Revenue Services.

sections.h2: How do revaluations and late tax interest affect a seller?
sections.html:
Every Connecticut town must revalue real property at least once every five years, so a house may be reassessed at a value that looks very different from the old one. Section 12-62 sets the five-year cycle, with a schedule prescribed by the state for each revaluation zone starting October 1, 2023.

If you disagree with a new value, you can appeal to the town's board of assessment appeals. A person aggrieved by that board's action can apply to the Superior Court no later than two months after the notice of the action was mailed, under section 12-117a.

Late payments are costly. The delinquent part of a tax carries interest at 18 percent per year from the due date, with a two-dollar minimum per installment that a town may choose to waive. When a house sells, the tax collector's balance, with that interest, normally comes out of the proceeds, so it helps to ask for a payoff figure early.

sections.h2: What should a Connecticut owner check before selling a home with debts?
sections.html:
Start with a list of what is owed and what is recorded. A title search will show mortgages and recorded liens, and the town tax collector can state the property tax balance. Then match each item against the rules above.

  1. Confirm whether you live in the house as your primary residence, because that decides whether the creditor shield can apply.
  2. Ask your assessor whether you qualify for any exemption or the circuit breaker credit before the next filing window.
  3. Request a payoff from each mortgage lender and from the tax collector.
  4. Check which conveyance tax exemption, if any, matches your sale, and note its code.
  5. Speak with a Connecticut attorney if a judgment creditor is involved, since an exemption claim in court has its own procedure.

A cash sale leaves these rules as they are. It only changes the timeline and removes repairs and showings.

faqs.q: Is there a property tax homestead exemption in Connecticut?
faqs.a: Connecticut's statutes use the word homestead for a creditor shield of $250,000 in section 52-352b(21). Property tax relief comes from named programs such as the circuit breaker credit and the exemptions in section 12-81. Ask your town assessor which one fits you.

faqs.q: Can a creditor force the sale of my Connecticut home?
faqs.a: A judgment creditor can pursue equity above the exempt amount, and a mortgage lender is not limited by the exemption at all. The exempt value is the fair market value minus liens, so equity under $250,000 in a primary residence is protected from ordinary judgment collection. An attorney can tell you how a particular debt is treated.

faqs.q: Do I have to live in the house for the exemption to count?
faqs.a: Yes. The statute defines a homestead as owner-occupied property used as a primary residence, so a rental or a second home does not qualify. A person who inherited a house and lives elsewhere should not assume the shield applies.

faqs.q: Who files the conveyance tax return when I sell?
faqs.a: The grantor, who is the seller, or the grantor's attorney or agent files Form OP-236. It is filed and any tax paid when the deed is recorded, with the town clerk or through myCTREC if the town takes part.

faqs.q: Where do I apply for a veterans or blind exemption?
faqs.a: Apply with your town assessor. Section 12-81 sets the dollar amounts, and the assessor's office has the forms and the filing dates for your town.
